activities.caption: place the December sun on the altitude scale
activities.name: edSunPlace

config.prompt: At 40° latitude the June noon sun sits at ~73°. Place the December noon sun on the scale (degrees):
config.why: 90 − 40 − 23.4 ≈ 27° — the 46° swing is a free seasonal switch: an overhang of d ≈ 0.58·h blocks the summer sun while covering only ~0.21·h of the winter window.
config.context: One square metre of south glazing under 500 W/m² winter sun at SHGC 0.6 delivers ~300 W of free heat — and the same square metre in July is an air-conditioning bill.

activities.anchor: not glass area on the elevation
activities.caption: bet first — the blinds' honest report card
activities.name: edGlassPredict

config.q: An all-glass facade ends its first summer with the blinds permanently down. What did the design get wrong?
choices: It treated daylight as glass area instead of useful daylight at the desk without glare
The glass was too thick to transmit light
config.why: Daylight is a flux to be admitted deliberately: glare and heat force the blinds, so the building delivers worse daylight AND a worse energy bill than a modest, well-oriented window would have.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the daylight depth rule
activities.name: edDaylightCloze

config.text: Daylight penetrates roughly %%0%% times the window-head height — a 3 m head gives %%1%% m of usable depth — and the %%2%% reflects high-angle sun onto the ceiling to push the bright zone deeper while shading the desk.
answers: two to two and a half
config.hint: One rule of thumb, one worked consequence, one horizontal baffle.

config.prompt: From buoyancy to flow — put the stack engine in order:
items: It vents through high-level atrium outlets
Replacement air is drawn through low-level inlets
The driving pressure runs about 0.5 Pa per metre of height at a 12 K difference
A five-metre atrium therefore offers about 2.5 Pa — small, but moving real air
config.why: That pressure doubles if either the height or the temperature difference doubles — which is why tall, section-first buildings ventilate themselves and single-storey slabs struggle without wind or fans.

activities.caption: true or false — tight vs leaky
activities.name: edTightJudge

statements.s: Airtightness and ventilation are opposites — seal for efficiency and accept stale air.
statements.why: Tight and ventilated beats leaky and accidental on every axis: the best-sealed buildings pair airtightness with deliberate supply.

statements.s: Uncontrolled infiltration through a leaky fabric wastes more heat than controlled ventilation ever needs.
statements.why: The ledger says so — which is why fabric-first comes before any equipment.

statements.s: Heat-recovery units keep most of the exhaust air's warmth before it leaves.
statements.why: Standard practice in cold climates: supply controlled, keep the warmth.

statements.s: Night purging recharges the concrete slab for tomorrow by discharging today's heat overnight.
statements.why: Air coupled to mass — vernacular windcatchers to Queensland verandas ran on exactly these physics.

activities.anchor: the wall section is the most consequential drawing in the building
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the U-value upgrade
activities.name: edUvalueSpot

config.prompt: One line of this wall-upgrade answer is wrong — click it:
lines: Add 150 mm of mineral wool (λ = 0.035): R = 0.15/0.035 ≈ 4.3 m²K/W.
Add surface resistances (~0.17) and total R ≈ 4.5, so U ≈ 0.22 W/m²K.
On a 20 K winter difference, heat loss falls from 40 to ~44 W/m².
config.correction: Heat loss falls from 40 to ~4.4 W/m² — TENFOLD, from one design decision.
config.why: Q = U·A·ΔT with U dropping tenfold gives a tenfold cut: 20 K × 0.22 ≈ 4.4 W/m². The wall section is the most consequential drawing in the building.

activities.anchor: paying a permanent energy bill for geometry
activities.caption: pair the hierarchy with its levers
activities.name: edHierarchyMatch

config.prompt: The cost-effective hierarchy runs the other way from the equipment catalogue:

pairs.left: equipment on an unshaded, west-glazed, poorly insulated building
pairs.right: a permanent energy bill for geometry that was free to fix

config.why: A watt avoided by orientation costs nothing to run for sixty years — the ordering is the argument: geometry and material choice first, machines last.
